chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. A pattern is first noticed in a list of numbers, then drawn with dots, then explained by the picture, and finally found again in sequences of shapes.

points.title: Notice, draw, explain
points.text: Every new sequence is first written out, then drawn with dots, and only then explained, because the book asks not just what the pattern is but why it happens.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's examples, a tool only where drawing or testing the sequence is the idea, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.

points.title: A picture is a reason
points.text: Adding odd numbers gives squares because an L-shape of dots wraps around a square grid. The picture works for a square of any size, so the pattern never stops.

points.title: Keeko's doubts
points.text: The common wrong ideas, such as 'adding odd numbers must give an odd number', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a picture or a check of the first few terms, never just a rule.

content.text: PATTERNS IN MATHEMATICS
content.publication_text: PATTERNS IN MATHEMATICS
lines: PATTERNS IN MATHEMATICS

content.text:
1. Look at the row of matchstick figures. Before reading on, guess: what would the next figure look like, and why?
2. Each figure is a little bigger than the one before, and it grows in the same way every time.
3. When something repeats or grows by a rule, that is a pattern, and a pattern lets us say what comes next.
4. This chapter is about finding such patterns in numbers and in shapes, and about explaining why they happen.

concepts.concept_name: Patterns are all around us

content.text:
Mathematics is, in large part, the search for patterns, and for the explanations as to why those patterns exist.
Such patterns indeed exist all around us, in nature, in our homes and schools, and in the motion of the sun, moon, and stars. They occur in everything that we do and see, from shopping and cooking, to throwing a ball and playing games, to understanding weather patterns and using technology.
The search for patterns and their explanations can be a fun and creative endeavour. It is for this reason that mathematicians think of mathematics both as an art and as a science. This year, we hope that you will get a chance to see the creativity and artistry involved in discovering and understanding mathematical patterns.

content.text:
Worked example: Name two patterns you meet in a day, one in nature and one at school.
1. Nature: day and night come back in turn, and the Moon changes shape in a fixed order.
2. School: the bell rings at fixed times, and the timetable repeats every week.
3. Each of these repeats by a rule, so each is a pattern.
Answer: Day and night, and the weekly timetable, are patterns.

concepts.concept_name: Why the explanation matters

content.text:
It is important to keep in mind that mathematics aims to not just find out what patterns exist, but also the explanations for why they exist. Such explanations can often then be used in applications well beyond the context in which they were discovered, which can then help to propel humanity forward.
For example, the understanding of patterns in the motion of stars, planets, and their satellites led humankind to develop the theory of gravitation, allowing us to launch our own satellites and send rockets to the Moon and to Mars; similarly, understanding patterns in genomes has helped in diagnosing and curing diseases, among thousands of other such examples.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if you notice that the Moon comes back to the same shape every month, is that enough for a mathematician?
2. No. Mathematics also asks why the pattern happens. The reason can then be used in other places.
3. Patterns in the motion of stars, planets and satellites led to the theory of gravitation, which lets us launch satellites and rockets.
4. Patterns in genomes have helped in diagnosing and curing diseases.

content.text:
Worked example: The Sun rises every day. Why does mathematics not stop at noticing this?
1. Noticing tells us only that the Sun comes back every day.
2. Mathematics asks why, and looks for a rule for the motion of the Sun, Moon and stars.
3. A rule found for one place can be used in other places, such as in launching satellites.
Answer: The reason gives a rule that can be used elsewhere, which a list of what happened cannot.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (Math Talk), p.2: Can you think of other examples where mathematics helps us in our everyday lives?
1. Think of buying fruit and vegetables: you count money and weigh things.
2. Think of a bus or train: speed tells you how long the trip takes.
3. Think of a floor tile design or the floor area of a room: shapes and numbers again.
Answer: Open discussion. Book examples: paying for fruits, vegetables, groceries; calculating speed of vehicles; designs or patterns in buildings; finding the area of a plot or one's own home.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (Math Talk), p.2: How has mathematics helped propel humanity forward? (You might think of examples involving: carrying out scientific experiments; running our economy and democracy; building bridges, houses or other complex structures; making TVs, mobile phones, computers, bicycles, trains, cars, planes, calendars, clocks, etc.)
1. Patterns in the motion of the Moon and planets led to the theory of gravitation.
2. That theory lets us launch satellites and send rockets to the Moon and Mars.
3. Patterns in genomes help doctors find and cure diseases.
Answer: Open ended: teacher-student discussion.

concepts.concept_name: Sequences that grow by a steady step

content.text:
Among the most basic patterns that occur in mathematics are patterns of numbers, particularly patterns of whole numbers:
0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...
The branch of Mathematics that studies patterns in whole numbers is called number theory.
Number sequences are the most basic and among the most fascinating types of patterns that mathematicians study.
Table 1 shows some key number sequences that are studied in Mathematics.
Table 1: Examples of number sequences
1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, ... (All 1's)
1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, ... (Counting numbers)
1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, ... (Odd numbers)
2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, ... (Even numbers)

content.text:
1. Predict first: what comes after 1, 3, 5, 7, 9? How did you know?
2. A list of numbers in a fixed order that follows a rule is a number sequence. The branch of mathematics that studies patterns in whole numbers is number theory.
3. All 1's: every term is 1. Counting numbers: add 1 each time. Odd numbers: add 2 each time from 1. Even numbers: add 2 each time from 2.
4. The rule is what tells us the next term, however far we go.

steps: Predict first: what comes after 1, 3, 5, 7, 9? How did you know?
A list of numbers in a fixed order that follows a rule is a number sequence. The branch of mathematics that studies patterns in whole numbers is number theory.
All 1's: every term is 1. Counting numbers: add 1 each time. Odd numbers: add 2 each time from 1. Even numbers: add 2 each time from 2.
The rule is what tells us the next term, however far we go.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the rule and the next term of 4, 7, 10, 13, 16.
1. The jump from each term to the next is 3.
2. So the rule is add 3 each time.
3. 16 + 3 = 19.
Answer: Add 3 each time; the next term is 19.

concepts.concept_name: Sequences whose jumps keep changing

lines: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, ... (Triangular numbers)

content.text:
1. Predict first: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. Does it add the same number each time?
2. No. The jumps are 2, 3, 4, 5, so each jump is one bigger. These are the triangular numbers.
3. Squares are 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3 and so on, giving 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Cubes are 1 × 1 × 1, 2 × 2 × 2 and so on, giving 1, 8, 27, 64, 125.
4. The next triangular number after 28 adds 8, giving 36.

concepts.concept_name: Sequences built from earlier terms

lines: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ... (Virahāṅka numbers)

content.text:
1. Predict first: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Look at 3, 5 and 8. How is 8 made from the two before it?
2. Each Virahanka number is the sum of the two terms before it: 3 + 5 = 8 and 5 + 8 = 13.
3. Powers of 2: multiply the last term by 2 to get 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Powers of 3: multiply the last term by 3 to get 1, 3, 9, 27, 81.
4. So a rule can add, or multiply, or use the earlier terms together.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students describe a number sequence as an ordered list formed by a rule, and state the rule for the All 1's, counting, odd and even number sequences.
Students find the rule for the triangular, square and cube number sequences, seeing that the jump between terms changes each time.
Students find the rule for the Virahanka numbers and for the powers of 2 and 3, where each term is made from the term or terms before it.
Students pick the rule for a sequence on the tool, test it on every term, and write the next terms.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (Math Talk), p.3: Can you recognise the pattern in each of the sequences in Table 1?
1. All 1's: every term is 1.
2. Counting numbers: add 1 each time.
3. Odd numbers: add 2 each time, starting from 1.
4. Even numbers: add 2 each time, starting from 2.
5. Triangular numbers: add 2, then 3, then 4, then 5, and so on.
6. Squares: 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, and so on. Cubes: 1 × 1 × 1, 2 × 2 × 2, and so on.
7. Virahanka numbers: each term is the sum of the two terms before it, for example 2 + 3 = 5.
8. Powers of 2: multiply the last term by 2. Powers of 3: multiply the last term by 3.
Answer: Yes, there is a pattern in each. All 1's: every term is 1. Counting: add 1. Odd: add 2 from 1. Even: add 2 from 2. Triangular: add 2, 3, 4, 5, ... Squares: 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, ... Cubes: 1 × 1 × 1, 2 × 2 × 2, ... Virahanka: each term is the sum of the two before it. Powers of 2: multiply by 2. Powers of 3: multiply by 3.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (Math Talk), p.3: Rewrite each sequence of Table 1 in your notebook, along with the next three numbers in each sequence! After each sequence, write in your own words what is the rule for forming the numbers in the sequence. All 1's) 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, ... Counting numbers) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, ... Odd numbers) 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, ... Even numbers) 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, ... Triangular numbers) 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, ... Squares) 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, ... Cubes) 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, ... Virahanka numbers) 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ... Powers of 2) 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ... Powers of 3) 1, 3, 9, 27, 81, 243, 729, ...
1. All 1's: the last term is 1, so the next three are 1, 1, 1.
2. Counting numbers: the last is 7, so the next three are 8, 9, 10.
3. Odd numbers: after 13 comes 15, 17, 19. Even numbers: after 14 comes 16, 18, 20.
4. Triangular: the last is 28, add 8, 9, 10 to get 36, 45, 55.
5. Squares: 8 × 8 = 64, 9 × 9 = 81, 10 × 10 = 100.
6. Cubes: 7 × 7 × 7 = 343, 8 × 8 × 8 = 512, 9 × 9 × 9 = 729.
7. Virahanka: 13 + 21 = 34, 21 + 34 = 55, 34 + 55 = 89.
8. Powers of 2: 64 × 2 = 128, 128 × 2 = 256, 256 × 2 = 512.
9. Powers of 3: 729 × 3 = 2187, 2187 × 3 = 6561, 6561 × 3 = 19683.

content.text:

concepts.concept_name: Why triangular, square and cube?

content.text:
1. Predict first: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. What shape could the dots make?
2. Triangular numbers: rows of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 dots stack into a triangle. Square numbers: n rows of n dots make a square grid. Cube numbers: n layers of an n by n square of blocks make a cube.
3. So the names come from the pictures, not by chance.

content.text:
Worked example: How many dots are in a triangle with 4 rows, and why is the number called triangular?
1. The rows have 1, 2, 3 and 4 dots.
2. 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.
3. The 10 dots stack in the shape of a triangle.
Answer: 10 dots; the rows stack into a triangle.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (Math Talk), p.5: Copy the pictorial representations of the number sequences in Table 2 in your notebook, and draw the next picture for each sequence!
1. All 1's: draw one more single dot.
2. Counting numbers: the sixth picture is 6 dots in a row.
3. Odd numbers: the sixth odd number is 11, so draw 11 dots.
4. Even numbers: the sixth even number is 12, so draw 12 dots in two rows of 6.
5. Triangular: add a sixth row of 6 dots, 15 + 6 = 21 dots.
6. Squares: a 6 by 6 grid of dots, 6 × 6 = 36 dots.
7. Cubes: a 6 by 6 by 6 cube of blocks, 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 blocks.
Answer: Next pictures: All 1's: 1 dot; Counting: 6 dots in a row; Odd: 11 dots; Even: 12 dots (two rows of 6); Triangular: 21 dots (triangle of 6 rows); Squares: 36 dots (6 by 6 grid); Cubes: 216 unit blocks (6 × 6 × 6 cube).

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (Math Talk), p.5: Why are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ... called triangular numbers? Why are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ... called square numbers or squares? Why are 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, ... called cubes? triangular) Why called triangular numbers? square) Why called square numbers? cubes) Why called cubes?
1. Dots 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 stack in rows of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, which makes a triangle.
2. Dots 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 fill a square grid, 1 by 1, 2 by 2, 3 by 3, 4 by 4, 5 by 5.
3. Blocks 1, 8, 27, 64, 125 build a cube, 1 by 1 by 1, 2 by 2 by 2, and so on.
Answer: Triangular: that many dots can be arranged in a triangle (rows of 1, 2, 3, ...). Square: that many dots form a square grid (n rows of n). Cubes: that many unit blocks form a cube (n by n by n).

content.text: This shows that the same number can be represented differently, and play different roles, depending on the context. Try representing some other numbers pictorially in different ways!

content.text:
1. Predict first: the number 6. Can you draw 6 dots in two different neat shapes?
2. Six dots make a triangle of rows 1, 2 and 3. Six dots also make a rectangle of 2 rows of 3.
3. So 6 is a triangular number, and it is also a number that can be shown as a rectangle.
4. The same number can be represented differently and play different roles.

content.text:
Worked example: Show 10 dots as a triangle and as a rectangle.
1. Triangle: rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4 dots, since 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.
2. Rectangle: 2 rows of 5 dots, since 2 × 5 = 10.
Answer: The same 10 dots make a triangle and a rectangle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a hexagon of dots with 1 dot, then a centre dot with a ring of 6. How many dots in all?
2. A centre dot and one ring of 6 dots make 1 + 6 = 7. Adding a ring of 12 more makes 7 + 12 = 19.
3. The rings grow by 6 each time: 6, 12, 18, 24. The pictures 1, 7, 19, 37 are called hexagonal numbers.

content.text:
Worked example: A hexagon cluster has a centre dot and one ring of 6 dots. How many dots are there after the next ring of 12 is added?
1. The centre dot and the first ring make 1 + 6 = 7 dots.
2. The next ring has 12 dots, and 7 + 12 = 19.
Answer: 19 dots.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q3 (Math Talk), p.5

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3 (Math Talk), p.5: You will have noticed that 36 is both a triangular number and a square number! That is, 36 dots can be arranged perfectly both in a triangle and in a square. Make pictures in your notebook illustrating this! (This shows that the same number can be represented differently, and play different roles, depending on the context. Try representing some other numbers pictorially in different ways!)
1. Triangle: rows of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 dots; 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 36.
2. Square: 6 rows of 6 dots; 6 × 6 = 36.
3. So the same 36 dots can be arranged both ways.
Answer: 36 dots as a triangle with 8 rows (1+2+...+8) and as a 6 by 6 square.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q4, p.5

content.text:
Figure it Out Q4, p.5: What would you call the following sequence of numbers? (Pictures of dot clusters labelled 1, 7, 19, 37.) That's right, they are called hexagonal numbers! Draw these in your notebook. What is the next number in the sequence?
1. The clusters are 1, 7, 19, 37: each is a centre dot with rings of 6, 12 and 18 dots around it.
2. The jumps are 6, 12, 18, so the next jump is 24.
3. 37 + 24 = 61, a centre dot with a fourth ring of 24 dots.
Answer: 61 (the sequence is called hexagonal numbers).

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q5, p.5

content.text:
Figure it Out Q5, p.5: Can you think of pictorial ways to visualise the sequence of Powers of 2? Powers of 3?
1. Powers of 2: a point, then a line segment, then a square, then a cube; each shape is two copies of the one before, joined.
2. The next shape is two cubes joined, a 4-dimensional cube, with 16 corners.
3. Powers of 3: a dot, then a triangle of 3 dots, then 3 triangles joined, then 3 of those joined.
Answer: Powers of 2 (book, p.6): a point, a segment, a square, a cube, a 4-D cube for 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 (solutions add 32). Powers of 3: e.g. a dot, a triangle (3), three triangles joined in a row (9), three such rows joined (27).

concepts.concept_name: Adding odd numbers: what do the sums show?

content.text:
Sometimes, number sequences can be related to each other in surprising ways.
Example: What happens when we start adding up odd numbers?
1 = 1
1 + 3 = 4
1 + 3 + 5 = 9
1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16
1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25
1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36
This is a really beautiful pattern!

Worked example: What happens when we start adding up odd numbers? 1 = 1; 1 + 3 = 4; 1 + 3 + 5 = 9; 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16; 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25; 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36; ...

4. 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16.
5. The sums 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 are the square numbers.

concepts.concept_name: The L-shapes that explain it

content.text:
Why does this happen? Do you think it will happen forever?
The answer is that the pattern does happen forever. But why? As mentioned earlier, the reason why the pattern happens is just as important and exciting as the pattern itself.
Visualising with a picture can help explain the phenomenon. Recall that square numbers are made by counting the number of dots in a square grid.
How can we partition the dots in a square grid into odd numbers of dots: 1, 3, 5, 7,... ? Think about it for a moment before reading further!
Here is how it can be done:
This picture now makes it evident that 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36.
Because such a picture can be made for a square of any size, this explains why adding up odd numbers gives square numbers.
By drawing a similar picture, can you say what is the sum of the first 10 odd numbers?
Now by imagining a similar picture, or by drawing it partially, as needed, can you say what is the sum of the first 100 odd numbers?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a 6 by 6 square grid of dots. Can you cut it into pieces of 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 dots?
2. Start at one corner with 1 dot. Wrap an L-shape of 3 dots around it, then an L of 5, then 7, and so on, each L having 2 more dots than the one before.
3. A square of any size can be cut this way, so adding odd numbers gives squares forever.
4. The picture works for the 10 by 10 and the 100 by 100 grid too.

content.text:
Worked example: How can we partition the dots in a square grid into odd numbers of dots: 1, 3, 5, 7,... ? (Think about it for a moment before reading further!)
1. Start at one corner with a single dot: 1 dot.
2. Wrap an L-shape of 3 dots around it: 1 + 3 = 4 dots.
3. Wrap an L-shape of 5 dots around that: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 dots.
4. Each new L-shape has 2 more dots than the one before: 7, 9, 11 and so on.
Answer: Cut the grid into nested L-shaped layers with 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 dots from one corner outwards.

3. So the sum of the first 10 odd numbers is 100.

concepts.concept_name: Up and then down: another way to get squares

content.text:
Let us look at the following pattern:
1 = 1
1 + 2 + 1 = 4
1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9
1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 16
1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 25
1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 36
This seems to be giving yet another way of getting the square numbers, by adding the counting numbers up and then down!

2. The pattern says an up-and-down sum to n is n × n.
3. 7 × 7 = 49.
Answer: 49.

lines: This seems to be giving yet another way of getting the square numbers, by adding the counting numbers up and then down!
Can you find a similar pictorial explanation?

content.text:
1. Predict first: tilt a 3 by 3 grid so a corner points up. How many dots are in each row?
2. The rows have 1, 2, 3, 2 and 1 dots, so 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9, the same 3 by 3 grid.
3. For any n, the tilted n by n grid has rows 1, 2, ..., n, ..., 2, 1, so the sum is n × n.

content.text:
Worked example: (Pattern: 1 = 1; 1 + 2 + 1 = 4; 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9; 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 16; 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 25; 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 36; ... This seems to be giving yet another way of getting the square numbers, by adding the counting numbers up and then down!) Can you find a similar pictorial explanation? (A 6 by 6 grid of dots is shown.)
1. 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, a diamond of rows of 1, 2 and 1 dots.
2. 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9, a diamond of rows of 1, 2, 3, 2 and 1 dots.
3. Tilt a square grid by a quarter of a turn: its rows along the diagonal count 1, 2, 3, up to the side length and back down.
4. So up-and-down sums of counting numbers also give squares.
Answer: Yes: arrange dots as a diamond whose rows have 1, 2, 3, ..., n, ..., 3, 2, 1 dots; it is an n by n grid seen along its diagonals, so n x n dots.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q1 (Try This), p.8

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (Try This), p.8: Can you find a similar pictorial explanation for why adding counting numbers up and down, i.e., 1, 1 + 2 + 1, 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1, ..., gives square numbers?
1. Draw a square grid of dots and tilt it so a corner points up.
2. Count the dots row by row: 1, then 2, then 3, up to n, then back down to 2 and 1.
3. The tilted grid is n by n, so the total is n × n.
Answer: Draw dots in a diamond: rows of 1, 2, 3, ..., n, ..., 2, 1 dots (the diagonals of an n by n grid), giving n x n dots.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (Try This), p.8: By imagining a large version of your picture, or drawing it partially, as needed, can you see what will be the value of 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 99 + 100 + 99 + ... + 3 + 2 + 1?

2. 100 × 100 = 10000.
Answer: 10,000

concepts.concept_name: Adding a sequence up: running totals

content.text: Sometimes, number sequences can be related to each other in surprising ways.
content.publication_text: Sometimes, number sequences can be related to each other in surprising ways.
lines: Sometimes, number sequences can be related to each other in surprising ways.

content.text:
1. Predict first: add up the even numbers step by step: 2, then 2 + 4, then 2 + 4 + 6. What do you get?
2. The running totals are 2, 6, 12 and then 20, because 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20.
3. Adding a sequence up step by step makes a new sequence, not the same one.
4. Different starting sequences give different results, so each one needs its own check.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the running totals of the sequence 3, 6, 9, 12.
1. The first total is 3.
2. 3 + 6 = 9.
3. 3 + 6 + 9 = 18.
4. 3 + 6 + 9 + 12 = 30.
Answer: The running totals are 3, 9, 18, 30.

concepts.concept_name: Adding neighbouring terms

content.text:
1. Predict first: add neighbouring counting numbers: 1 + 2, then 2 + 3, then 3 + 4. What do you get?
2. The sums are 3, 5, 7, 9, the odd numbers after 1.
3. Each sum is the smaller number twice plus 1, which is why it is odd.
4. A picture or a reason shows whether the pattern goes on, and a check of the first few terms alone does not.

Worked example: Add each pair of neighbouring even numbers: 2 and 4, 4 and 6, 6 and 8, 8 and 10.

2. 4 + 6 = 10.
3. 6 + 8 = 14.
4. 8 + 10 = 18.
Answer: The sums are 6, 10, 14, 18, going up by 4 each time.

media.title: What do we get when we keep adding the next number?
media.context: Patterns in Mathematics. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The numbers three, six, nine and twelve are added up one at a time, and the total after each step is written down. Each total holds all the numbers so far. Keeko doubts this and says the totals are the same list again.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a running total is the last total plus the next number, so each total holds every number so far. Watch for students who write the sequence itself instead of the totals.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

media.title: What happens when we add neighbouring even numbers?
media.context: Patterns in Mathematics. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The even numbers two, four, six, eight and ten are added in neighbouring pairs, and the sums are lined up to see how they change. Each sum is four more than the one before. Keeko doubts this and says the sums go up by two, like the even numbers.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q3 (Try This), p.8

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3 (Try This), p.8: Which sequence do you get when you start to add the All 1's sequence up? What sequence do you get when you add the All 1's sequence up and down? up) Add the All 1's sequence up up and down) Add the All 1's sequence up and down
1. Add the All 1's sequence up: 1, then 1 + 1 = 2, then 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, then 4, and so on.
2. These running totals are 1, 2, 3, 4, ..., the counting numbers.
3. Add it up and down: 1, then 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, then 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5, then 7.
4. These are 1, 3, 5, 7, ..., the odd numbers.
Answer: Adding the All 1's sequence up gives the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, ... Adding it up and down gives the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, ...

content.text:
Figure it Out Q4 (Try This), p.8: Which sequence do you get when you start to add the counting numbers up? Can you give a smaller pictorial explanation?
1. Running totals of the counting numbers: 1, then 1 + 2 = 3, then 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, then 10.
2. These are 1, 3, 6, 10, ..., the triangular numbers.
3. A small picture: rows of 1, 2, 3, 4 dots stack into a triangle of dots.
Answer: The triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, ... Picture: rows of 1, 2, 3, 4 dots stack into a triangle.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q5 (Try This), p.8

content.text:
Figure it Out Q5 (Try This), p.8: What happens when you add up pairs of consecutive triangular numbers? That is, take 1 + 3, 3 + 6, 6 + 10, 10 + 15, ... Which sequence do you get? Why? Can you explain it with a picture?
1. 1 + 3 = 4, 3 + 6 = 9, 6 + 10 = 16, 10 + 15 = 25.
2. The sums 4, 9, 16, 25 are the square numbers.
3. Picture: a triangle of 6 dots and a triangle of 3 dots turned over fit together into a 3 by 3 square.
Answer: 4, 9, 16, 25, ... the square numbers. Two consecutive triangles of dots fit together to make a square.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q6 (Try This), p.8: What happens when you start to add up powers of 2 starting with 1, i.e., take 1, 1 + 2, 1 + 2 + 4, 1 + 2 + 4 + 8, ... ? Now add 1 to each of these numbers, what numbers do you get? Why does this happen? sums) 1, 1+2, 1+2+4, 1+2+4+8, ... add 1) Add 1 to each
1. Running totals of powers of 2: 1, 1 + 2 = 3, 1 + 2 + 4 = 7, 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15, 31.
2. Add 1 to each: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
3. These are the powers of 2.
4. Why: each new shape is two copies of the one before, so one more than the total so far is the next power.
Answer: Sums: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, ... Adding 1 to each: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ... the powers of 2.

7. Picture: a centre dot with six triangles around it.
Answer: 7, 19, 37, 61, 91, ... the hexagonal numbers.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q8 (Try This), p.9: What happens when you start to add up hexagonal numbers, i.e., take 1, 1 + 7, 1 + 7 + 19, 1 + 7 + 19 + 37, ... ? Which sequence do you get? Can you explain it using a picture of a cube?

3. 1 + 7 + 19 = 27.
4. 1 + 7 + 19 + 37 = 64.
5. These are the cube numbers; each hexagonal number is one layer of the next cube.
Answer: 1, 8, 27, 64, ... the cube numbers.

concepts.concept_name: Shapes that grow one step at a time

content.text:
Other important and basic patterns that occur in Mathematics are patterns of shapes. These shapes may be in one, two, or three dimensions (1D, 2D, or 3D), or in even more dimensions. The branch of Mathematics that studies patterns in shapes is called geometry.
Shape sequences are one important type of shape pattern that mathematicians study. Table 3 shows a few key shape sequences that are studied in Mathematics.
Table 3: Examples of shape sequences

content.text:
Worked example: The shapes triangle, square and pentagon are in a sequence. Draw the next two.
1. The rule is one more side each time.
2. After the 5 sides of the pentagon comes a shape with 6 sides, a hexagon.
3. Then comes a shape with 7 sides, a heptagon.
Answer: A hexagon, then a heptagon.

concepts.concept_name: Stacking squares and triangles, and the Koch snowflake

content.text:
1. Predict first: a big square made of little squares, 1 by 1, then 2 by 2, then 3 by 3. What is the rule?
2. Stacked squares add a row and a column. Stacked triangles add a new bottom row of little triangles.
3. The Koch snowflake replaces each line segment by a speed bump, so the segments get tinier and tinier and the shapes become hard to draw.

content.text:
Worked example: A stack of squares is 3 by 3 little squares. What is the next stack, and how many little squares does it have?
1. Each stack adds a row and a column, so the next stack is 4 by 4.
2. 4 × 4 = 16.
Answer: A 4 by 4 stack with 16 little squares.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (Math Talk), p.11: Can you recognise the pattern in each of the sequences in Table 3? Regular Polygons) Pattern? Complete Graphs) Pattern? Stacked Squares) Pattern? Stacked Triangles) Pattern? Koch Snowflake) Pattern?
1. Regular polygons: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 sides, one more side each time.
2. Complete graphs: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 lines.
3. Stacked squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 little squares.
4. Stacked triangles: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 little triangles.
5. Koch snowflake: 3, then 3 × 4, then 3 × 4 × 4, then 3 × 4 × 4 × 4 segments.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q2 (Math Talk), p.11

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (Math Talk), p.11: Try and redraw each sequence in Table 3 in your notebook. Can you draw the next shape in each sequence? Why or why not? After each sequence, describe in your own words what is the rule or pattern for forming the shapes in the sequence.
1. Regular polygons: add one more side.
2. Complete graphs: add a new point and join it to every earlier point.
3. Stacked squares: add a row and a column; stacked triangles: add a new bottom row.
4. Koch snowflake: replace every segment by a speed bump; the next shape can be drawn, but the segments become very tiny.
Answer: Open ended. Typical: next polygon has one more side; K7 (7 points all joined); stacked squares 6 × 6; stacked triangles with 6 rows; Koch snowflake gets very hard to draw as segments become tiny.

concepts.concept_name: Sides of regular polygons

content.text:
Often, shape sequences are related to number sequences in surprising ways. Such relationships can be helpful in studying and understanding both the shape sequence and the related number sequence.
Example: The number of sides in the shape sequence of Regular Polygons is given by the counting numbers starting at 3, i.e., 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, .... That is why these shapes are called, respectively, regular triangle, quadrilateral (i.e., square), pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon, decagon, etc., respectively.
The word 'regular' refers to the fact that these shapes have equal-length sides and also equal 'angles' (i.e., the sides look the same and the corners also look the same). We will discuss angles in more depth in the next chapter.

content.text:
1. Predict first: one matchstick triangle uses 3 sticks. A row of 2 triangles sharing a side uses 5. How many sticks for a row of 3?
2. The counts 3, 5, 7, 9 go up by 2 each time, the odd numbers after 1.
3. So counting the sticks in a shape sequence gave a number sequence.
4. The other sequences in Table 3 have such relationships too, and a relation helps us study both.

content.text:
Worked example: How many matchsticks make a row of 5 triangles that share sides?
1. One triangle uses 3 sticks, and each new triangle adds 2 sticks.
2. The counts are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
3. The fifth count is 9 + 2 = 11.
Answer: 11 matchsticks.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q1 (Try This), p.11

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (Try This), p.11: Count the number of sides in each shape in the sequence of Regular Polygons. Which number sequence do you get? What about the number of corners in each shape in the sequence of Regular Polygons? Do you get the same number sequence? Can you explain why this happens? sides) Number of sides corners) Number of corners why) Why?
1. Sides: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, the counting numbers starting at 3.
2. Corners: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, the same sequence.
3. Each corner is where two sides meet, so a closed shape has as many corners as sides.
Answer: Sides 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, ... (counting numbers starting with 3). Corners: the same sequence. In any closed figure the number of sides equals the number of corners (vertices).

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (Try This), p.11: Count the number of lines in each shape in the sequence of Complete Graphs. Which number sequence do you get? Can you explain why?
1. K2 has 1 line, K3 has 3, K4 has 6, K5 has 10, K6 has 15.
2. These are the triangular numbers.
3. Why: the new point joins to all the earlier points, adding 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 lines in turn.
Answer: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, the triangular numbers.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3 (Try This), p.12: How many little squares are there in each shape of the sequence of Stacked Squares? Which number sequence does this give? Can you explain why?
1. Count the little squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
2. These are the square numbers.
3. Each shape is n rows of n little squares, so n × n of them.
Answer: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, the square numbers; each shape is n rows of n little squares.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q4 (Try This), p.12

content.text:
Figure it Out Q4 (Try This), p.12: How many little triangles are there in each shape of the sequence of Stacked Triangles? Which number sequence does this give? Can you explain why? (Hint: In each shape in the sequence, how many triangles are there in each row?)
1. Count the little triangles row by row: the rows have 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 triangles.
2. Add the rows: 1, then 1 + 3 = 4, then 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, then 16, then 25.
3. These are the square numbers, because adding odd numbers gives squares.
Answer: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, the square numbers. The rows have 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 triangles (odd numbers), so the totals are sums of odd numbers, which are squares.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q5 (Try This), p.12

content.text:
Figure it Out Q5 (Try This), p.12: To get from one shape to the next shape in the Koch Snowflake sequence, one replaces each line segment by a 'speed bump'. As one does this more and more times, the changes become tinier and tinier with very very small line segments. How many total line segments are there in each shape of the Koch Snowflake? What is the corresponding number sequence? (The answer is 3, 12, 48, ..., i.e., 3 times Powers of 4; this sequence is not shown in Table 1.)
1. Shape 1 has 3 segments.
2. Each segment becomes 4, so shape 2 has 3 × 4 = 12.
3. Shape 3 has 12 × 4 = 48, shape 4 has 48 × 4 = 192, shape 5 has 192 × 4 = 768.
4. The sequence is 3 times the powers of 4.
Answer: 3, 12, 48, 192, 768, ... which is 3 times the powers of 4.

concepts.concept_name: What we found about patterns

content.text:
Mathematics may be viewed as the search for patterns and for the explanations as to why those patterns exist.
Among the most basic patterns that occur in mathematics are number sequences.
Some important examples of number sequences include the counting numbers, odd numbers, even numbers, square numbers, triangular numbers, cube numbers, Virahāṅka numbers, and powers of 2.
Sometimes number sequences can be related to each other in beautiful and remarkable ways. For example, adding up the sequence of odd numbers starting with 1 gives square numbers.
Visualising number sequences using pictures can help to understand sequences and the relationships between them.
Shape sequences are another basic type of pattern in mathematics. Some important examples of shape sequences include regular polygons, complete graphs, stacked triangles and squares, and Koch snowflake iterations. Shape sequences also exhibit many interesting relationships with number sequences.

1. Our opening question is settled: the matchstick row grows by a rule, and a rule lets us say what comes next.
2. Number sequences such as counting, odd, even, triangular, square, cube, Virahanka and powers of 2 follow rules, and pictures explain how they relate, as odd numbers adding up to squares.
3. Shape sequences hide number sequences in their counts.
4. Still open for you: find a pattern of your own and explain why it happens.

objectives.objective_text: Students say that mathematics is largely the search for patterns, and name patterns from nature, home, school, games and the sky.
Students explain that mathematics looks for the reason a pattern exists, and that a reason found in one place can be used elsewhere, as with gravitation and genomes.
Students give their own examples of mathematics in everyday life and in the progress of humanity.
Students describe a number sequence as an ordered list formed by a rule, and state the rule for the All 1's, counting, odd and even number sequences.
Students find the rule for the triangular, square and cube number sequences, seeing that the jump between terms changes each time.
Students find the rule for the Virahanka numbers and for the powers of 2 and 3, where each term is made from the term or terms before it.
Students pick the rule for a sequence on the tool, test it on every term, and write the next terms.
Students draw the dot pictures of the counting, odd and even number sequences, and tell how each next picture grows from the one before.
Students see that triangular numbers stack in a triangle of dots, square numbers fill a square grid and cube numbers build a cube of blocks.
Students build the next dot picture of a sequence on the tool and name the number it shows.
Students show that a number such as 6 can be drawn in two different ways, and say that the same number can play different roles depending on the picture.
Students build a hexagonal number picture as a centre dot with rings of 6, 12 and more dots, and find each next number by adding the next ring.
Students draw 36 as a triangle and as a square, find the next hexagonal number, and picture the powers of 2 and 3.
Students add the first few odd numbers one at a time, see that the sums are square numbers, and say the pattern is worth explaining.
Students cut a square grid of dots into nested L-shaped layers of 1, 3, 5, 7, ... dots, explain why the pattern goes on forever, and find the sum of the first 10 and 100 odd numbers.
Students wrap L-shapes of odd numbers of dots around a corner on the tool and read the square number each time.
Students add the counting numbers up and then down for the first few lines, see squares, and predict the next line.
Students tilt a square grid of dots so that its rows count 1, 2, 3, ..., n, ..., 3, 2, 1, and use it to explain why adding up and down gives squares.
Students build up-and-down sums as a diamond of dots on the tool and read off the square number.
Students form the running totals of a sequence and see that they make a new number sequence.
Students add each pair of neighbouring terms of a sequence and find the new sequence, checking it on the first terms.
Students combine sequences on the tool by running totals and sums of neighbours, and name the sequence that results.
Students describe the rule for the regular polygon and complete graph sequences of Table 3 and name geometry as the study of patterns in shapes.
Students describe the rule for the stacked squares, stacked triangles and Koch snowflake sequences, and say why the snowflake soon becomes hard to draw.
Students draw the next shape of each Table 3 sequence on the tool and state its rule in their own words.
Students link the shapes triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon and so on to the counting numbers starting at 3, and say what regular means.
Students count the matchsticks in a row of triangles to get a number sequence, and see that other shape sequences have beautiful relationships with number sequences.
Students count sides, lines, little squares, little triangles and segments on the tool and name the number sequence each count gives.
Students restate that mathematics is the search for patterns and their reasons, name the main number sequences, and say how pictures explain relations among sequences and link shapes to numbers.

Book item: You will have noticed that 36 is both a triangular number and a square number! That is, 36 dots can be arranged perfectly both in a triangle and in a square. Make pictures in your notebook illustrating this! (This shows that the same number can be represented differently, and play different roles, depending on the context. Try representing some other numbers pictorially in different ways!)

Book item: What would you call the following sequence of numbers? (Pictures of dot clusters labelled 1, 7, 19, 37.) That's right, they are called hexagonal numbers! Draw these in your notebook. What is the next number in the sequence?

Book item: The number of sides in the shape sequence of Regular Polygons is given by the counting numbers starting at 3, i.e., 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, .... That is why these shapes are called, respectively, regular triangle, quadrilateral (i.e., square), pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon, decagon, etc., respectively.

Book item: How many little triangles are there in each shape of the sequence of Stacked Triangles? Which number sequence does this give? Can you explain why? (Hint: In each shape in the sequence, how many triangles are there in each row?)

Book item: To get from one shape to the next shape in the Koch Snowflake sequence, one replaces each line segment by a 'speed bump'. As one does this more and more times, the changes become tinier and tinier with very very small line segments. How many total line segments are there in each shape of the Koch Snowflake? What is the corresponding number sequence? (The answer is 3, 12, 48, ..., i.e., 3 times Powers of 4; this sequence is not shown in Table 1.)
